title: Closed-Loop Load Generation Hiding Queueing Delay (Coordinated Omission)
pattern: A load generator or latency benchmark issues each request only after the previous one on the same thread completes (synchronous send in a loop, fixed pool of blocking workers), paces requests with a relative `sleep(interval)` after completion, and measures latency from the actual send time instead of the time the request was scheduled to be sent.
why_bad: When the server stalls, the generator stalls with it: no requests are issued during the stall, so the queue that real independent clients would build never forms, and the recorded samples omit exactly the requests that would have waited longest (coordinated omission). Relative sleeps compound the effect; the real inter-request gap becomes `latency + interval + timer slop`, so offered load drops precisely when the server is most stressed. Reported percentiles can be orders of magnitude better than what users experience.
detection: In benchmark or load-test code: a loop that performs a blocking send/await and then `thread::sleep`/`tokio::time::sleep` with a constant `Duration` without computing `next_deadline - Instant::now()` from an absolute schedule; or N threads/tasks each running `loop { blocking_send() }` with no independent arrival schedule; in either case, latency recorded as `start.elapsed()` where `start` is taken at actual send rather than at the intended send time, with no coordinated-omission correction (e.g. HdrHistogram `record_correct`).
counterexample: Closed-loop tests whose declared goal is capacity at a fixed concurrency ("how many requests/s do 64 connections sustain") and that do not report per-request latency percentiles as user-facing latency; open-loop generators that dispatch at precomputed absolute timestamps from an arrival schedule and measure from those timestamps; polling loops that are not load generators.
source: Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* (2017), Ch. 1, p. 13; Brendan Gregg, *Systems Performance* (2013), Ch. 1, §1.9, p. 12 and Ch. 12, p. 593; Richard L. Sites, *Understanding Software Dynamics* (2021), Ch. 26, §26.6, p. 327; Michael T. Nygard, *Release It!* (2007), Ch. 9, §9.2, p. 178.
